Timeline/Precursor to AI

Precursor to AI · 1816–1899

Literary and philosophical precursors

Long before researchers built learning machines, writers asked what it would mean to love one, depend on one, or lose control of one.

Three nineteenth-century works give those questions memorable forms: an artificial woman mistaken for a person, machines that might surpass humanity, and a chess player that turns on its maker. They belong to the cultural history of artificial intelligence.

1816 · E. T. A. Hoffmann · Short story

The Sandman: seeing a person in a machine

In The Sandman (Der Sandmann), Nathanael becomes infatuated with Olimpia, whom he believes to be a young woman. She is an automaton. Her attentive silence and sparse replies let him imagine an understanding companion; her eventual exposure destroys that illusion.

The story gives an early fictional form to anthropomorphism: attributing human feelings and understanding to something artificial. Read alongside today’s conversational systems, it raises a familiar question: how much of a seemingly intimate exchange comes from the listener’s own expectations?

That comparison is an interpretation. Nathanael does not knowingly choose a machine partner, and the story does not establish that Olimpia has feelings of her own.

About the date: The story appeared in autumn 1816 in Nachtstücke, whose first volume bore the advance date 1817. The English reading link below is John Oxenford’s 1844 translation, where the names appear as Nathaniel and Olympia.

  • Read The Sandman in English
  • Read Nachtstücke in German
  • Berlin State Library: manuscript and first-edition dating

1872 · Samuel Butler · Satirical novel

Erewhon: when our creations might surpass us

The society in Erewhon has suppressed advanced machinery. Its justification appears in “The Book of the Machines,” which considers whether machines could develop consciousness, evolve beyond human abilities, and make people dependent on them.

The unsettling possibility is gradual dependence as well as open conflict. Humans build, repair, and improve machines; the argument asks whether those activities might eventually serve a more powerful mechanical order. This makes the novel relevant to questions about human control and technological dependence.

Butler presents competing arguments within a satire. A character’s warning is not automatically the author’s settled prediction. In his revised-edition preface, Butler traces this part of the novel to his essay Darwin among the Machines, published on June 13, 1863.

Where to read: The novel first appeared in March 1872. In the revised edition linked below, “The Book of the Machines” occupies chapters XXIII–XXV; chapter numbering differs between editions.

  • Read Erewhon, including Butler’s account of its origins
  • Smithsonian Libraries: the 1872 edition
  • Read Darwin among the Machines in Canterbury Pieces

1899 · Ambrose Bierce · Short story

Moxon’s Master: intelligence without obedience

The story opens with an argument about whether a machine can think. Later, the narrator watches Moxon play chess against an automaton. After being checkmated, the machine appears to attack and strangle its creator.

Bierce brings together three enduring themes: games as a display of intelligence, uncertainty about a machine’s inner life, and a creator’s loss of control. The title itself invites the reader to reconsider who is master of whom.

The ending leaves room for doubt. Years afterward, the narrator is less certain about his explanation of the death. The story’s apparent machine rebellion remains filtered through a fallible witness.

About the date: The story first appeared in the San Francisco Examiner on April 16, 1899. It was later included in the 1910 edition of Can Such Things Be? The reading edition below records both dates.

  • Read Moxon’s Master, with publication notes (PDF, 10 pages)

c. 1951 · A documented connection

Turing explicitly refers to Erewhon

There is a direct connection between Butler’s fiction and Turing’s discussion of machine intelligence. In Intelligent Machinery, A Heretical Theory, Turing considers machines exceeding human intellectual abilities and eventually taking control. He explicitly refers to Samuel Butler’s Erewhon in the closing paragraph.

The archive dates the lecture approximately 1951. It is a separate work from the 1950 paper on the imitation game featured in the research timeline. The citation belongs to the later lecture; it does not establish that every argument in Butler’s novel shaped Turing’s research.

  • King’s College, Cambridge: original lecture archive
  • Read Turing’s reference, printed page 475 (PDF)

How these works connect to the research

These works document questions people asked before AI became a research field. Their fictional machines are not evidence of functioning AI, and thematic resemblance alone does not prove that a later researcher read or cited them.

For a thematic reading path, compare Hoffmann’s imagined listener with ELIZA’s appearance of conversation, Bierce’s chess player with research on learning and search in games, or Butler’s machine future with Turing’s questions about evaluating intelligence. These are comparisons across ideas; Turing’s explicit reference to Butler above is a documented citation.
